title: Using a regional climate model and a machine learning algorithm for farmer - herder conflict prediction in the Sahel region
abstract: Climate variability and environmental stress are increasingly recognized as key factors influencing conflict dynamics in vulnerable regions. This study explores the relationship between climate variability and conflict risk in northern Nigeria's Sudano–Sahelian region by combining regional climate modeling with machine learning techniques. High-resolution climate projections were produced using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) regional climate model to simulate essential climate variables, including precipitation, temperature, and soil moisture. These data were used to develop environmental stress indicators such as rainfall anomalies, drought frequency, and the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI). Past conflict event data from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) project and the Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP) were integrated with climate variables and socioeconomic factors to train machine learning models for prediction. The findings show that drought severity, rainfall variability, and soil moisture deficits are among the most significant predictors of conflict risk in this area. Of the tested algorithms, the Random Forest model provided the highest accuracy, with an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of about 0.86, surpassing traditional regression methods. Spatial maps highlight several conflict hotspots in northern parts of the Sudano–Sahelian region where climate stress and population pressure are especially intense. The results suggest that climate-induced environmental stress can escalate competition over land and water resources, raising the likelihood of resource-based conflicts, especially between farming and pastoral groups. By combining regional climate modeling with machine learning-based prediction techniques, this study offers a new framework for understanding and foreseeing climate-related conflict risks in climate-sensitive areas. The findings underscore the potential for integrating climate science and data-driven conflict prediction to support early warning systems and guide proactive policies that enhance resilience and prevent conflicts in the Sahel and similar vulnerable regions.
problem: Existing climate-conflict prediction studies are limited by their reliance on coarse global climate data and the failure to integrate high-resolution climate models with machine learning algorithms, hindering the ability to forecast conflict risks driven by localized environmental stress.
method: This paper proposes a predictive framework that integrates a regional climate model with machine learning algorithms to forecast farmer-herder conflict risk by combining high-resolution climate projections with historical conflict and socioeconomic data.
task: The task is to predict farmer-herder conflict risk in the Sudano-Sahelian region of northern Nigeria by integrating high-resolution regional climate model outputs with machine learning algorithms trained on historical conflict data and environmental indicators.
innovation: This paper presents a novel framework that integrates a regional climate model with a machine learning algorithm to create a predictive system for forecasting farmer-herder conflict risks in the Sudano-Sahelian region of Nigeria.

Atmospheric data for the study were generated using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) Model, a widely used regional climate model developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The WRF model is designed to simulate atmospheric processes at high spatial and temporal resolutions and is widely applied in regional climate modeling studies (Skamarock et al., 2019).

Climate variables extracted from the WRF model include: precipitation, surface temperature, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, wind velocity. These variables were used to construct climate stress indicators relevant to conflict dynamics.

Land-surface data were obtained from the Community Land Model (CLM), which forms part of the Community Earth System Model (CESM) developed by NCAR. The CLM simulates interactions between land surface processes and atmospheric systems, including vegetation dynamics, soil hydrology, and land-use changes (Lawrence et al., 2019).

Although the Sudano-Sahelian region is located inland, ocean-atmosphere interactions play an important role in influencing rainfall variability in West Africa. Climate phenomena such as El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and Atlantic sea surface temperature anomalies are known to influence rainfall patterns in the Sahel (Giannini et al., 2008). Ocean data used in the study will therefore be obtained from the ARGO global ocean observation system, which collects real-time measurements of ocean temperature, salinity, and pressure using autonomous drifting floats (Roemmich et al., 2019). These datasets were used to provide boundary conditions for regional climate simulations and to improve the realism of climate projections.

Nigeria represents a particularly important case study for examining climate-conflict dynamics. Northern Nigeria lies within the Sudano-Sahelian climatic zone, which is characterized by high temperatures, low rainfall, and recurrent drought conditions. Over the past several decades, the region has experienced significant environmental changes, including declining rainfall variability, desert encroachment, and increasing land degradation. These environmental challenges have contributed to increasing tensions between farmers and pastoralists competing for diminishing natural resources (Adelphi, 2019). As climate variability intensifies, these conflicts are expected to become more frequent and severe.

This study focuses on the Sudano-Sahelian region of northern Nigeria, located approximately between longitudes 4°E and 14°E and latitudes 10°N and 14°N. The region forms part of the broader Sahelian ecological zone, characterized by semi-arid climatic conditions, highly variable rainfall, and recurrent drought events. Annual rainfall in the zone typically ranges between 300 mm and 600 mm, with the majority of precipitation occurring during the short rainy season from May to September (Ati et al., 2010).

The simulated results indicate that northern parts of the Sudano-Sahelian region exhibit higher environmental stress levels compared with southern parts of the zone. States such as Sokoto and Borno record the highest drought severity, with SPI values below –1.5, indicating severe drought conditions. These areas also show lower soil moisture indices, suggesting reduced water availability for crop production and pasture regeneration. Rainfall anomalies across the region range from –44 mm to –85 mm per year, indicating persistent precipitation deficits that may negatively affect agricultural productivity. The results also show that drought events occur approximately four to six times per decade, supporting earlier findings that drought recurrence is a major environmental stressor in the Sahelian region (Mortimore, 2010).
